source.title: A generalization of the Collatz problem and conjecture

accepted.question_text: Let n be a positive integer and define an iteration by replacing n with n/2 when n is even and with 3n + 1 when n is odd, then repeating the same rule on each new value. Does this iteration eventually reach the number 1 for every positive integer chosen as the initial value?

evidence.quote: Consider the following operation on an arbitrary positive integer: * If the number is even, divide it by two. * If the number is odd, triple it and add one.
Conjecture 1 This process will eventually reach the number 1, irrespective of which positive integer n is chosen initially.
This Conjecture is simple to state but so difficult to prove that the issue of its validity is still open.

accepted.question_text: For integers b >= 2 and m >= 1, define a generalized Collatz iteration on a positive integer x as follows: if x is divisible by b, replace x by x/b; if x is not divisible by b, replace x by (b^m + 1)x + b^m - (x mod b^m). Starting from any positive integer S0, must the resulting sequence always eventually reach the Collatz-type finite cycle 1, 2b^m, 2b^(m-1), ..., 2b, 2, 3b^m, 3b^(m-1), ..., 3b, 3, ..., b - 1, ..., b, 1?

evidence.quote: Define the function f(n, b, m) as follows (n, m = 1, 2, ..; b = 2, 3, ...): f(n, b, m) = n/b if n ≡ 0 (mod b) , (3) f(n, b, m) = (bm + 1)n + bm − (n mod bm ) if n 6= 0 (mod b) .(4)

An obvious question arises: since our mapping is a natural generalization of the Collatz one and considering the result of the above Proposition, may we hope that a generalized Collatz conjecture hold true, namely that for any b, m, S0 the limit cycle (17) is eventually reached?

Of course hope is hope, not reality: realistically one should expect to find easily a large number of counter-examples, namely a large number of limit cycles different from the Collatz type one given in (17) (divergences also could possibly arise, but we never found one).
Indeed for m = 1 it is easy to find counter-examples even for small values of b, S0 :

accepted.question_text: For integers b >= 2 and m = b - 1, define a generalized Collatz iteration on a positive integer x by replacing x with x/b when x is divisible by b and replacing x with (b^m + 1)x + b^m - (x mod b^m) when x is not divisible by b. Does every sequence generated from every positive initial integer eventually reach the number 1?
accepted.context_brief: Main m = b - 1 generalized Collatz conjecture

evidence.quote: Define the function f(n, b, m) as follows (n, m = 1, 2, ..; b = 2, 3, ...): f(n, b, m) = n/b if n ≡ 0 (mod b) , (3) f(n, b, m) = (bm + 1)n + bm − (n mod bm ) if n 6= 0 (mod b) .(4)
Conjecture 2 If m = b − 1 the sequence (5) shall eventually reach the number 1, irrespective of which positive integer is chosen initially.

Remark Note that for b = 2 this is just the original Collatz conjecture. We have tested this conjecture for a large number of values of b and S0. We offer C=1 for a counter-example, C= 100 for a proof.

accepted.question_text: For integers b >= 2 and m >= 1, define the generalized Collatz iteration on a positive integer x by replacing x with x/b when x is divisible by b and replacing x with (b^m + 1)x + b^m - (x mod b^m) when x is not divisible by b. Call the starting values of the form S0 = s b^N with s < b^m and N >= 0 trivial, since these are already covered by the proved convergence result. In the parameter regimes m = 1 with b equal to 5, 7, or 8; m = 2 with b > 2; and m > 2 with b >= 2, can one find starting values outside that trivial family whose trajectories do not reach the Collatz-type cycle 1, 2b^m, 2b^(m-1), ..., 2b, 2, 3b^m, 3b^(m-1), ..., 3b, 3, ..., b - 1, ..., b, 1, for example by entering a different finite limit cycle or by diverging?
accepted.context_brief: Counterexample search in unbroken parameter regimes

evidence.quote: Define the function f(n, b, m) as follows (n, m = 1, 2, ..; b = 2, 3, ...): f(n, b, m) = n/b if n ≡ 0 (mod b) , (3) f(n, b, m) = (bm + 1)n + bm − (n mod bm ) if n 6= 0 (mod b) .(4)

Of course this set can be trivially extended to an infinite set considering all the values S0 = s bN , s < bm, N = 0, 1, 2, .. For all these initial values the sequence (5) obviously converges to the number 1 and thus the limit cycle (17) due to the above Proposition and to the rule (3).
Let us call ’trivial’ all these values of S0 (and ”non-trivial ” the values outside this set).

Many other counter-examples can be found for m = 1; note however that we found none not only for b = 2 (this was expected since that is the original Collatz map) but also for other small values of b as b = 5, b = 7, b = 8 (and this was quite unexpected).
To our surprise, for m = 2, b > 2 and for m > 2, b ≥ 2 we have found no other counter-example...

we do not dare to propose a new general conjecture of the Collatz type (however we dare to offer C= 1 for each of the first 100 counter-examples in the cases m = 1, b = 5, 7, 8; m = 2, b > 2; m > 2, b >= 2 ).
